note: Recorded platform time-service readings and the classification each one must produce. Every raw value is what the named operating-system interface reports; nothing here is a measurement this build took of a clock it does not own, and no case describes an authenticated time protocol the platforms do not expose.

platforms.reads: The kernel clock discipline the system time service maintains. `modes` is zero, so the call reports and changes nothing, and it needs no privilege. The return value is the time state; the status word says which discipline is running; `maxerror` is the kernel's own bound in microseconds.

cases.name: this machine, recorded 2026-09-17
the service has not settled the clock yet
nothing is keeping the clock

platforms.reads: The same kernel model, through the adjtimex status, maintained by whichever of systemd-timesyncd, chronyd or ntpd the host runs. The Linux and macOS status bits and time states are the same values, which is why one classifier serves both.

cases.name: systemd-timesyncd has the clock
a pulse-per-second reference is disciplining the phase
a leap second will be inserted
the clock hardware itself failed
a bound looser than the tolerance is not evidence

platforms.reads: The W32Time service's own status report. `Source` names what is keeping the clock, `Leap Indicator` is the NTP field of the same name, `Stratum` says whether the reference is attached to this machine (one) or reached over the network (two to fifteen), and a stratum of one is read as a reference clock only when the source also names one, and the bound is the root dispersion plus half the root delay, which is how NTP bounds a reading taken across a round trip. Both halves are required: reading a missing round trip as zero would understate what the service claims.
